findings.title: Ebb beside feared outflow

findings.mechanism: Before: The focus diagnoses reluctance to let possessed matter leave. This contact changes expenditure from a one-way subtraction model into an analogy tested against re-creation after material loss. findings.reader_payoff: The reader sees that the fear presumes irreversibility, while the nearby resurrection argument does not treat material disappearance as the last possible state.
findings.containment: The packet supplies bodily disassembly, reawakening, new creation, and capacity; I infer that this sequence analogically discredits expenditure-as-irreversible-loss. findings.title: A middle between closure and release

In 17:110, prayer is not to be voiced at either extreme, and a path between them is sought. This contact qualifies the focus's contrast between holding and spending: the relevant closure can be fear-governed rather than every limit on outflow. Structural cue: 17:110 uses paired prohibitions followed by an imperative to seek a path between them.
findings.reader_payoff: The reader can see a distinction between closing access from fear and limiting an action while keeping a route open.
findings.containment: The packet supplies loudness, lowered speech, an intermediate state, and a path; I infer a general distinction between calibrated release and fear-driven closure. A live alternative confines the calibration strictly to prayer volume. The context may concern prayer volume only and may not generalize to material giving. This comparison does not establish a general rule for every form of expenditure.

findings.title: Human possession under unshared sovereignty
findings.claim: The closing denial of any partner in sovereignty and any ally required by weakness lets the focus's imagined transfer of control read as a stress test: dependent possessors constrict from fear, unlike unshared divine sovereignty.
findings.mechanism: Before: The hypothetical simply says humans would administer divine assets badly. After: It demonstrates why mercy's absolute sovereignty cannot be modeled as human possession: dependent possessors protect themselves by constriction, while the closing ملك is unshared and free of compensating need. The focus's tamlikūna carries a possible sovereignty reading. In 17:111 the kingdom is explicitly unshared, dependence through weakness is denied, and magnification closes the sequence. Their contact shifts the focus from a hypothetical about poor human administration toward a comparison between dependent human possession and sovereignty that is not held from need. Structural cue: The pericope closes by repeating كان in two negations around شريك في الملك and ولي من الذل, then intensifies the command to magnify.
findings.reader_payoff: The reader can see the counterfactual as more than bad asset management: it tests what happens when dependent holders imagine absolute control.
findings.containment: The packet supplies denied partnership, sovereignty, denied dependence, and magnification; I infer that 17:100's لو is a stress test of transferred absoluteness. A live alternative reads 17:111 as a separate doxology rather than the resolution of the ownership hypothetical. The source preserves the alternative that 17:111 is a separate doxology. No claim is made that the closing verse explicitly explains the focus or that human ownership is the only reading.

epistemic.reason: The repeated sovereignty root and all 17:111 role coordinates match the packet. The connection to the focus is attributed by a legacy-unbound HFT source, with the separate-doxology reading retained.
